A 37-year-old woman noted persistent low back pain following a minor motor vehicle accident in 1982.
She was felt to have post-traumatic stress syndrome. The patient was treated with butalbital for pain and diazepam and baclofen for muscle spasms.

There was pronounced rigidity and tenderness of axial muscles, with marked lordosis. She could walk with assistance, but the gait was rigid and slow. Her movements were often interrupted by painful spasms of paraspinal and limb girdle muscles.

extractions.value: We considered the diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome. EMG studies were normal except for continuous motor unit activity, mainly in the paraspinous muscles. Exaggerated exteroceptive reflex responses were elicited. Both exteroceptive reflexes and continuous motor unit activity were abolished or markedly reduced following intravenous infusion of 10 mg diazepam, which did not produce any change in mental status. Radiographs of the spine showed marked lumbar lordosis, and MRI was otherwise unremarkable. CSF analysis was normal (protein, 28 mg/dl; IgG, 1.8 mg/dl; R value, 0.56; and no oligoclonal bands). Metabolic screening, including random and fasting blood glucose levels, was normal. A trial of clonidine was initiated on the patient’s discharge from the hospital, but was discontinued when she did not improve. Diazepam was increased to 130 mg daily, with mild reduction in spasms and rigidity. Indirect immunofluorescent screening of serum revealed autoantibody reactive with normal human cerebellum in a pattern consistent with GABAergic terminals. Serum titers of GAD-like immunoreactivity fell from 1:1,280 to 1:80 during plasmapheresis. There was marked incremental improvement in EMG studies at each point tested. The areas of evoked exteroceptive reflex responses declined dramatically (figure 1). There was more than a fivefold decline in the size of the response in paraspinal muscles, from 26.2 to 4.98 uVsec, by the third plasma exchange (figure 2). Observed clinical response was equally striking: after two exchanges, rigidity had decreased, paraspinal muscles were palpably less stiff, and the patient was able to sit up unassisted. During the course of plasmapheresis, her gait became progressively more fluid and she was able to walk without spasms. Subjective improvement fluctuated and lagged behind observed measures but did not return to the preadmission state. Two weeks after discharge, she reported improvement to nearly normal functioning (a level of 2 on her 10-point scale, 1 being normal) and she had reduced diazepam dosage by 10 mg.

Indirect immunofluorescent screening of serum revealed autoantibody reactive with normal human cerebellum in a pattern consistent with GABAergic terminals. Immunoperoxidase staining was carried out on sections of fixed rat or guinea pig brain incubated in 1:160 to 1:1,280 dilutions of patient serum overnight. After rinsing, sections were incubated in biotinylated antihuman IgG, reacted with avidin-biotin-peroxidase complex (ABC) (Vector), and developed with diaminobenzidine.

extractions.value: abductor pollicis brevis, biceps brachii, lumbar paraspinal, biceps femoris, tibialis anterior
extractions.quote: Surface recordings were made simultaneously from five muscle groups (abductor pollicis brevis, biceps brachii, lumbar paraspinal, biceps femoris, and tibialis anterior) using a TECA Mystro EMG.

extractions.value: Exteroceptive reflexes were recorded using a modification of the technique described by Meinck et al. Surface recordings were made simultaneously from five muscle groups (abductor pollicis brevis, biceps brachii, lumbar paraspinal, biceps femoris, and tibialis anterior) using a TECA Mystro EMG. The recording gain was adjusted to obtain a well-defined signal from each channel. A frequency window of 20 Hz to 2,000 Hz was used in all recordings. The responses were full-wave-rectified and four responses were signal-averaged. Each response was obtained by delivering a train of five stimuli to the median nerve at the wrist at a rate of 200 Hz. The stimulus was delivered at the threshold for motor activation of the thenar muscles.
